newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Azerbaijan calls for Nagorno-Karabakh peace.
newsitem.headline: Azerbaijan calls for Nagorno-Karabakh peace.

text.p: Azerbaijan President Heydar Aliyev appealed to Armenia on Monday to agree terms for a peace settlement over Nagorno-Karabakh and end a conflict threatening to cause friction at a European security summit.

Aliyev told more than 50 leaders at the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) summit that Armenia was intent on pursuing independence for Nagorno-Karabakh, an enclave with an ethnic Armenian majority surrounded by Azeri territory.

The president said his framework peace proposal called for recognition of Azerbaijan's territorial integrity, an assurance of a high degree of autonomy for Nagorno-Karabakh and security guarantees for all the enclave's population.
"It is regrettable that the Republic of Armenia refuses to accept such a formula...It refuses to accept the territorial integrity of the Azerbaijani republic," Aliyev told the summit.
He said Armenia was pursuing the "non-legitimate claims for the independence of Nagorno-Karabakh".
"We shall never agree to these claims and we cannot allow the creation on the territory of Azerbaijan of a second Armenian state," he said. "We do not want war. We want peace."

Up to one million Azeri refugees have lived in tent camps since ethnic Armenians drove Azeris out of the enclave in a six-year war triggered by Nagorno-Karabakh's independence declaration in 1988. Some 10,000 people were killed in the fighting.

A fragile ceasefire has existed since May 1994, but both sides have failed to agree a peace settlement. Talks in Helsinki mediated by the 11-nation Minsk Group, a body set up by the OSCE, broke down last month.
The OSCE summit in Budapest in 1994 agreed to prepare a multinational peacekeeping force for Nagorno-Karabakh, but deployment cannot go ahead until both sides agree peace.

OSCE sources said the dispute could disrupt efforts to put together a final declaration at the Lisbon summit. Azerbaijan could hinder, or block, a final summit document if it fails to win affirmation of its territorial integrity.
